en: Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter,
the Exposition of the Extent of Future Narratives.
Now, for the purpose of introducing the subsequent future narratives, the extent is described in due order.

Thus, while Maṅgalabhañjana remained there and the people of Vraja were once again distressed here, Vṛndā and Pūrṇimā, their hearts unfulfilled, withdrew to a secluded place after the crowd had dispersed. For it was thus: immediately after Keśimathana’s departure from Vraja for Mathurā, Vṛndā and Pūrṇimā—unable to bear witnessing the suffering of those people—had gone to stay in a land far removed from them, accompanied by Madhumangala.
For a long time he dwelt in the seclusion of the forest retreats;
and then, as these two were conversing on various matters, their conversation turned out this way:
"When the battle with Śālva broke out, our settlement was besieged by that distress."
Then, knowing each of those events, Vṛndā spoke with tears: "O Blessed One, what will happen next? I cannot fathom the interval that lies ahead.
Then Pūrṇimā spoke, her voice choked with emotion: "And for me, my very body no longer stirs, overwhelmed by a grief that has extinguished all light."
"How much more so for one standing before you? But let that be; what of one who does not stand before you?
[5] Vṛndā said: "By means of your own *yogamāyā*, for the sake of concealing yourself, why is your knowledge repeatedly obstructed by you while assuming the guise of an ascetic?
[6] Pūrṇimā said: "Just as it is with you, who possess the form of the power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*)."
[7] Vṛndā said: And how is that?
[8] Pūrṇimā said: That certain power of Hari, named *prīti*, which consists of the states beginning with *rati*, *prema*, *praṇaya*, *rāga*, *anurāga*, and culminating in *mahābhāva*, shines forth;
she is powerful everywhere and perpetually deludes even Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the supreme refuge for those such as ourselves. For example—
"Then, not seeing the calves, Kṛṣṇa returned to the sandbank and also searched for the cowherd boys everywhere in the forest. [BhP 10.13.16] Vṛndā said: "Even this is not seen to be universal," [9]
But the cause is not grasped.
[10] That power manifests itself by becoming manifest even within Śrī Kṛṣṇa, precisely through its proximity to those bhaktas who possess full-moon-like love.
[11] Vṛndā said: "What has come of this being introduced?
[12] "Through the association of us as well with those who dwell in the glorious Vraja and possess supreme full-moon-like love."

"What more need be said? Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself has said: 'Even you, who are sometimes submerged and sometimes emerging in the current of the Gaṅgā of divine love, attain both consciousness and unconsciousness [of Him].
Vṛndā said: 'In that case, what is the course for our hope?

Pūrṇimā said: 'For one like you, who even in dreams practices only lamentation, on the very next night—after this night has passed—a certain person whose identity is concealed will give this book to me.'"
He placed it in his hand, saying,
"Examine this," and having spoken thus, he wandered away somewhere.
Therefore, you must become like eyes for me, whose eyes are intent on shedding tears that are difficult to restrain due to the impurity of the cataract of grief.
[15] But Vṛndā, bowing to him, said:
"Upon leaves of golden hue, with incomparable colors resembling the jewels of the Lord of the Immortals, his body is seen on all sides even in deep darkness as if strewn with gems."

We know that this book, which possesses a string of clear pearls fastened upon it, has appeared here of its own accord like Kṛṣṇa himself, manifesting the splendor associated with his garments and other ornaments.
(A garland) [16] Pūrṇimā said joyfully: "In that case, this most worthy object will surely bring about a conscious realization in our minds; therefore, read it at once."
[17] Vṛndā, together with her circle of young women, proceeded to that place of recitation.

First, observing the names and letters arranged outside, she described it thus: "Here is the portion of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*—the very essence of fortune—which has been secured; it is the meditable section from the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Padma Purāṇa*, ever vigilant in bestowing a share of its glorious portions."
"From time to time, some other things were also collected for the sake of various provisions.
[18] Then, saying "Now let the first [chapter] be recited," after the account of Pūrṇimā, Vṛndā recited: [19] Now, the verses from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:
"When that sinful one had fallen and Saubha was struck down by the mace..."
O King, kettledrums sounded in the sky, struck by the hosts of gods;
meanwhile, Dantavakra approached in a rage, seeking vengeance against his friends.
Śrī Śuka said:
The evil-minded one acted as a friend in absentia toward Śiśupāla, Śālva, and Pauṇḍraka, even though they had departed for the next world.
O Great King, a single foot-soldier was seen, enraged and brandishing a mace in his hand; that great being made this earth tremble with his feet.
Seeing him approaching in that manner, Kṛṣṇa quickly took up his mace, leaped down from his chariot, and checked him as the shore checks the ocean. (10.38.1–3), and so forth. And at the end of that—
Kṛṣṇa also struck him in the center of the chest with his heavy mace, Kaumodakī;
his heart pierced by the mace, he vomited blood from his mouth.
Stretching out his hair, arms, and legs, he fell lifeless upon the earth;
then, O King, as all beings looked on, a most subtle and wondrous black light entered him, just as it did at the slaying of the King of Cedi.
But his brother Vidūratha, overwhelmed with grief for his brother, arrived panting with sword and shield, desiring to slay him.
And as he was rushing forward, O king of kings, Kṛṣṇa severed his head— complete with its crown and earrings— with his razor-edged discus.
Having thus slain Saubha, Śālva, and Dantavakra along with his younger brother— all of whom were unbearable for others— he was praised by gods and men.
Surrounded by the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, he entered the decorated city.
(10.78.8–13, 15) [20] Pūrṇimā said: "This was understood here:
when the slaying of Śālva was connected [to the narrative], then Dantavakra, having taken up his mace and being fully armored, was wandering about there."
"Even by Śrī Kṛṣṇa's mace, one may be driven out," he said.
Then, at the conclusion of that, his female disciple Vṛndā addressed the Blessed One:
"This matter is beyond my comprehension."

When indeed did the one named Dantavakra, whose abode was far away, learn of that undertaking called the slaughter of Śālva which had begun at that very moment? Or how could he have learned of it, and how did he enter that region from his own distant land like a deity at that very instant?
And even there, being armed with a mace, how is it that he arrived on foot, all alone?

[22] Pūrṇimā said: "An excellent question has been asked; however, please find pleasure in your own words even by reading what follows immediately after that. [23] Vṛndā read that as well—the prose passages from the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*: "Then, having heard that Śiśupāla had been slain, Dantavaktra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa."

Having heard that, Kṛṣṇa mounted his chariot and went to Mathurā to fight him. A battle took place for a day and a night between Dantavakra and Vāsudeva at the gate of the city of Mathurā on the bank of the Yamunā; Kṛṣṇa struck him with his mace, and he fell with all his limbs crushed like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
...as if lifeless, fell upon the surface of the earth. Thus it was said.
[24] Having had this read, Vṛndā asked: "This pair of Purāṇas appears, on the contrary, to be mutually contradictory.
[25] To this, Pūrṇimā—whose understanding was now fulfilled by the various words she had received—replied: "No, no!"
However, it is impossible that the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata speaks incoherently;

furthermore, since it is possible for it to form a single syntactical unity with another Purāṇa, a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is not logical. Thus, by the principle that a syntactical unity otherwise unaccounted for must be established, this is understood: that just as in the case of Śālva, when he did not attend the Rājasūya along with Śiśupāla, [the earth shook] due to the excellence of his movement which caused the trembling of the earth.

Having been recited as one who is renowned, a great being, an ocean, and one who split the mountain with his thunderbolt, he has suddenly attained a state of supreme power; thus, when he is recognized, the propitiation of the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) is inferred.

In that very [recitation], the connection between the striking of the foot and the collection of counter-measures for one who is about to be expelled by a flash of light is considered difficult to reconcile.
And in that case, the great power of the chariot of Muramathana—which possesses a speed exceeding the course of one's desires—is understood to be fully possible;

likewise, the assistance of Śrī Nārada is awaited, who is capable of perceiving the playful combat desired by Hari, who possesses the swiftness of thought, and who is expert in maneuvering through various movements.
Thus it is indeed stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam: [26]
Seeking to avenge his friends, the evil-minded Dantavakra departed in a rage against Śiśupāla, Śālva, and Pauṇḍraka as well.
Thus, here Śālva is also included in the count. And in the *Padma Purāṇa*, it is stated: "But Kṛṣṇa, having heard that...

However, regarding the statement in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*—"A being of great courage was seen" (*BhP* 10.78.2)—it is understood from the words of Śrī Nārada that although he was seen, his true nature was known [by Kṛṣṇa].

And so it was: having heard that Śrī Gopāla had not yet departed from Indraprastha after slaying Śiśupāla, Dantavakra set out for Mathurā and stood on the road, intending to oppose him by engaging in a duel since he was free from rivals there.

But having perceived earlier that he had already set out for Dvārakā, Dantavakra became uncertain and fell into a cycle of deliberation; indeed, he was [advised] by the venerable Nārada himself, who is the very essence of the bliss of divine play, regarding that wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi).
He took note of the slaying of Śālva and other events;

and the Lord of Dvārakā, through that narration and the manifestation of the direct perception of his arrival, traveled there by means of that chariot as if it were his own mind along the path of the past.
Surely these two opinions, being complete, shall become one;
this too will become clear today or tomorrow through further distinction.
Let the matter be investigated again and again with ever-increasing depth.
[27] Then Vṛndā recited; and as she was reciting, she seemed as if she were dancing. Therein, as before, was that prose passage.

For instance: Kṛṣṇa, having slain him and crossed the Yamunā, went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement; there he saluted his former parents and comforted them, and was embraced by them with throats choked with tears.
Having prostrated before all the elder cowherds and comforted them, he gratified those present there with jewel-ornaments and other gifts. Thus it is said.
[28] Having read this, Vṛndā, with rising tears, asked again: "Is even this in agreement with the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata?
[29] Pūrṇimā, her mind full of joy, said: "Let the Uttara-vibhāga be seen.
[30] Vṛndā, having again uttered "Śrī-Bhāgavata," recited:
"Seeing them thus suffering, the best of the Yadus consoled them with loving messengers, saying, 'I shall return.
[BhP 10.38.35] Thus spoke Pūrṇimā; these words were spoken at the time of his departure from Mathurā.
[32] Vṛndā spoke again:
"O dear one, you all go to Vraja; we shall come to see our kinsmen who are pained by affection, after having provided happiness for our friends."
[33] Pūrṇimā spoke: A few days after the killing of Kaṃsa, this speech of Śrī Kṛṣṇa was heard by the assembly of Vraja, headed by the Lord of Vraja, in Śrī Vraja.
[34] Vṛndā recited again:
"Having slain Kaṃsa, the adversary of all the Sātvatas, in the midst of the arena..."
"What Kṛṣṇa has told you upon coming here, he will make true," and also:
"In no long time Acyuta will come to Vraja;
the Blessed Lord, the master of the Sātvatas, will bring joy to his parents."
Pūrṇimā said: "This has been understood as the message from Uddhava.
And here, the phrase 'to see' (draṣṭum) means that the very act of seeing is the human goal (puruṣārtha).

As for the statement 'he will perform what is pleasing to his parents,' the meaning is that even though their sole human goal is He, He will fulfill their cherished desire in the form of His own eternal fondling."
[36] "Let it be recited again on the full moon day.
[37] Vṛndā recited:
"Having fixed my entire mind upon Me, with all other mental fluctuations abandoned,"
"Constantly remembering me, you shall soon come to me.
[BhP 10.47.36] [38] This very verse from the *Śrīmad-Uddhava-saṃdeśa* is also [relevant here].
In this context, the word "me" (*mām*) occurs three times—beginning with the phrase "in me" (*mayi*)—and therein, first, the word "Kṛṣṇe" [is used].
Even though the two words "mā" and "mām" are specifically prescribed [in the previous verse], intending their recurrence through a change of case-ending,
the attainment of the Self is intended to occur precisely through the form of Kṛṣṇa at the conclusion of this section;
however, let something else be stated.
[39] Vṛndā said: Furthermore, there is a certain statement from the *Harivaṃśa*: "I am that very one who wanders in the forest among the cows with the cowherds;
full of joy, I shall roam at will like an elephant. Thus it is said.
[40] Pūrṇimā said: This reply of the conqueror of Kaṃsa to Ugrasena following the slaying of Kaṃsa is marked by my commentary as being the witness for this explanation.

[41] Then Vṛndā, making this very statement her subject, as if dancing, spoke these words: "Truly, the word of Him whose resolve is ever true shall not fall into falsehood. And if I consider the account of His return to Vraja from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam itself, which is composed for the delight of the ears,"
Then that alone would be the most pleasing.
On the full moon day, she, filled with eagerness, said: "Write a reply to that letter;
perhaps it might even be delivered."
[43] Vṛndā said joyfully: "There is something; as it is said in the Śrī-Bhāgavata itself:
'O lotus-eyed one, whenever you departed...'"

Or else, O Acyuta, let us go to the Kurus or the Madhus out of a desire to see our friends; for there, a single moment would be like ten million years to us, just as it is for those deprived of the sun by their eyes.
[44] Pūrṇimā said: "This is the entry into Dvārakā by the Lord of Śrī-Dvārakā following the imminent Bhārata war, and the speech of the subjects of Dvārakā.
[45] Here Vṛndā made this request: 'Let this verse be clarified.
[46] Then Pūrṇimā described it, beginning with 'Just as [he went to] the Kurus,' regarding the Kuru country."
Likewise, "madhūn" is an indication of the Madhurā region;
furthermore, he establishes that even the friends remained in Vraja after the departure for Dvārakā—just as it is said:
"O best of the Kurus, the Lord Balabhadra has mounted the chariot."
Longing to see his friend, he set out for Nanda’s Gokula with great yearning.
Vṛndā said: "This [meeting] might have been expected to occur at some other time, but not specifically after the battle with Dantavakra."

[48] Pūrṇimā reflected and instructed her, "Look again. [49] Vṛndā spoke once more: "Yes, yes! Once again, a verse from the Śrī-Bhāgavata is being realized: 'O friends, do you not remember us, who acted for the sake of our own kin?'"
"Those who have departed and delayed, their minds intent on destroying the enemy faction...
[BhP 10.82.41] Having had this read aloud, Vṛndā spoke again: "What is to be inferred from this?

Pūrṇimā replied: "This refers to the journey to Kurukṣetra; it was a clever way for Śrī Rāma’s brother to destroy the enemy faction in order to protect the slender bodies of those in Vraja, who were the objects of his own affection, from suffering."
Thus it was vowed as the limit:
the destruction of the enemy faction shall extend only as far as the encounter with Śatadhanvan and Dantavakra;
for immediately thereafter, the taking up of weapons by oneself would have been relinquished.
Therefore, this view of the *Padma Purāṇa*, which is the abode of all happiness, is understood as a portion (*bhāga*) of the glorious *Bhāgavata*.
Consequently, let someone indeed believe in the slaying of Dantavakra somewhere [within it].
Immediately after that, however, the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Vraja must certainly be considered.
Having said this, the Goddess spoke again: "Is there anything else?

[53] Vṛndā said: "In the same way, with the attire of a traveler," and so forth—this refers precisely to the statement from the *Harivaṃśa* concerning the dialogue between Śrī Rāma, who had arrived from Vraja, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as previously shown.

He recited: [54] Then Pūrṇimā spoke regarding his intention: "In this matter, when Rāma’s younger brother questioned his elder brother Rāma—who had come from Vraja—in private about the welfare of every single soul in Vraja; and when Kṛṣṇa said, 'I wish for the welfare of all those for whose welfare you desire it.'"
Therefore, having obtained a reply, the auspiciousness of their future reunion was also envisioned there by both of them;
for if there were indifference toward that [reunion], there would likewise be indifference toward this [present state].

Then Vṛndā, though her mind was pierced by that [news], spoke with uncertainty: "How could his return to Vraja not be free from artifice? He has made his speech a dwelling-place, like the *Padma Purāṇa*. [55]
And that essence of the Purāṇas, Pūrṇimā, spoke: "They indeed praise this Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam as the 'ornament upon the shoulder of Śrī Kṛṣṇa';
yet it does not venture to reveal its own secret openly."

And that [concealment] was due to the strength of his pride and his sense of independence; it was for the purpose of veiling the minds of those who were indifferent to him—being dependent on their desire for various other riches—and for the purpose of greatly intensifying the longing of those in Gokula who, out of love, considered themselves distinct from him and were deprived of clearly hearing his own specific desires.
[57] Vṛndā said: "The veiling of the minds of the former [residents] was appropriate."
"But for what purpose has this longing arisen in others?
[58] Pūrṇimā replied:
"When love enters into a state of union with longing,"
One should worship that which is born of the limbs and called Hari-saṅga at that time, and not at any other time.
[59] Vṛndā, smiling with effortless ease, said: "How many years after his birth did this most auspicious event—the arrival at Vraja from the city of Dvārakā by the slayer of Kaṃsa—occur?
[60] Pūrṇimā, with focused intent, replied: "According to the Bhārata tradition, it occurred sixty years after Yudhiṣṭhira’s extensive reign following the Bhārata war."

It appears that Śrī Viṣṭaraśravā (Kṛṣṇa), being distinguished by his age as being slightly younger than Arjuna, would have reached fifty-seven years of age at that time, since Yudhiṣṭhira was three years his junior. However, considering the period of his arrival in Vraja— prior to the thirteen-year forest exile and before the battle with Sālva, Dantavakra, and Dhūrvaṇa— only forty-four years remain.

Subsequent to that, regarding the protection of the earth by one residing in the city [of Dvārakā] through another manifestation, since it is impossible for the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* to be in agreement with the *Mahābhārata* as they differ in their perspectives, the assumption of a difference between the *kalpas* (cosmic cycles) is the only logical conclusion;
however, that [difference] is not the operative factor here.

"Then let that be; let what is at hand be introduced. Vṛndā said: "After the prose passage beginning with 'Kṛṣṇa, having slain him...', two verses from the *Padma Purāṇa* were written and recorded as follows:"
On the delightful bank of the Kālindī, which was covered with sacred trees,
Keśava sported incessantly with the cowherd women.
"Clad in the dress of a cowherd, Hari dwelt there for two months, indeed through the very joy of delightful pastimes and bound by the essence of love. Thus it is said.
Then Vṛndā questioned him regarding its underlying purport.

[63] Regarding the statement "Pūrṇimā said with the cowherd women" (*gopa-nārībhiḥ*), since the rule *nṛ-narayor vṛddhiś ca* prescribes the feminine suffix only when referring to a genus (*jāti*), it is understood that she spoke with "women belonging to the cowherd caste" (*gopa-jātibhir nārībhiḥ*).
Furthermore, this is seen in the words of Śrī Śukla addressed to Kardama concerning Devahūtī in the Third Skandha, as well as in the corroborating statement from the Mṛtyuñjaya-saṃhitā.

One should remember Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who incessantly enchants thousands of cowherd maidens in the delightful Vṛndāvana, their faces framed by the weight of their full, high breasts shimmering with pearl necklaces. Thus it is said.
And in the *Gautamīya*:
"The supreme one, the sole teacher of the three worlds, was worshipped with the flowers of devotion by thousands of cowherd girls whose eyes were as long as lotus petals."

By the phrase "when the night of Brahmā had passed," which is distinct from what was previously stated, and by the word "unceasingly" (*aniśam*), [it is shown that] when those women— who were created by me through *yoga-māyā* for the sake of deceiving the husbands of the real *abhīrīs* among those who considered themselves such— were being manifested again according to the direction stated in "they did not feel envy toward Kṛṣṇa," etc., the delusion regarding their status as the wives of others among the former [women] was subsequently removed.
One proceeds toward the release from contraction;
and that must necessarily be understood there,
for it is there that all virtues are celebrated as being conducive to modesty.
For instance, in the *Harivaṃśa*, this praise of him by the venerable Nārada acted like an ear-ornament for the assemblies of the Yādavas:

"Where modesty (*hrī*) and fortune (*śrī*) abide, there is humility (*sannati*); where fortune is, there is humility; likewise, modesty, fortune, and humility always reside in the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa. (*HV* 2.101.73)

[64] By the phrase "in this very way, through the bliss of delightful pastimes" and by the phrase "with the essence of abundant love," it is shown here in Vraja that the bliss of those pastimes is the fulfillment of all desires and that they consist of various essences of love.
And thus, that which was previously brought about among them through Māyā— the absence of envy— is likewise established.

And that [knowledge] would be fully realized even among these women whose secrets were manifest through their great separation from Him. Furthermore, there is the knowledge— “I am His eternal beloved”— which the Lord sports within the multitude of cowherd girls, just as He did with the daughter of Janaka, in order to manifest the power of the love of His beloveds and to delight those dear to Him, by means of His descent in play whose nature is necessarily such at every kalpa.
Although she was covered,
she was nevertheless unable to conceal her affections.
For that love, being so utterly dependent on those divine pastimes, would protect her devotion to him even during the state of falling into the hands of another, just as it did for her.
Do not think otherwise: that very same one will indeed be the one who, having pacified that state which is of the nature of suffering even in the future, will bring them together.
For it is well known from His own words: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them.
Indeed, those words were intended precisely for the purpose of uniting them after first arranging the torment of their husbands.
He honors [them]; for what is intended there is this: that the very nature of the devotees' desires is manifested as my own form.
And that "nature of their kind" belongs to those of their class in this very way: "O, when will such good fortune ever be ours?"

That which is perceived as being another's wife might become false through the effortless occurrence of a bad dream, whereas her status as one's own wife would be true through the wakefulness of haste;
let such be the way for women who are passionate toward another man in this case.
Elsewhere as well, the state of being a wife to one similar to him is always desired.
And thus it was intended by those very [gopīs]:
"What auspicious deed did this flute perform, that it now drinks for itself the nectar of Dāmodara’s lips even from the gopīs?
Alas! Is the noble son now staying in Madhupurī?"
O gentle one, does he remember his father’s house, his kinsmen, and the cowherds?
Does he ever speak of us, his maidservants;
and when will he place that arm, fragrant with aloe-wood, upon our heads?

In this context, there exists a hidden conceit on their part: "We belong to him who is indeed designated by our term 'Noble Son' (ārya-putra)," and even while thinking, "We are his maidservants," they wonder, "When will he himself openly accept us? Here, by the word "Noble Son" (ārya-putra), his status as a husband is suggested; and by the phrase "us, who are maidservants" (naḥ kiṅkarīṇām) and so forth, it is further suggested that his acceptance of them will likewise become manifest.

[67] This very journey of the Blessed One to Vraja, and following that journey to Vraja, the manifestation of His own belonging to them (svīyatā) is indeed the cause of auspiciousness; this was indicated by the Blessed Son of the Lord of Vraja Himself:
"They sustain their lives with great difficulty, somehow or other..."
By means of messages concerning my return, let the cowherd women, who are devoted to me, [be informed].
Thus, those words indeed convey to them their own possession [of him];
and even in that state of possession, they convey his singular nature, as well as the fact that he has returned after being dispersed and filled [with longing] due to his distant stay.
And this being so, it demonstrates that just as their separation is unbearable, so too is the report of their belonging to another;
or rather, it makes her realize that this [separation] is even greater than that, thereby leading to the conclusion:
"Therefore, I shall certainly cause her to perish."
[68] Vṛndā said: "O long-lived one, that which is meditated upon by you shall surely come to pass. [69] Pūrṇimā also said:
"She is among the women of Vraja who have surpassed the Goddess of Fortune, for their lips have been tasted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
Let those devoid of devotion consider as real that state of being the leftovers of others arising from marriage and the like—which is merely illusory;
alas, fie on them! But what of those who are devoted to it, who desire it with stability and even listen to its praises? GC_2,3.3.

Vṛndā asked: "If his stay here were for two months, how could there have been an entry into Dvārakā together with the hosts of Yadus who had assembled on the field of battle—along with the regions and their forms—due to the observation of [the verse beginning] 'How indeed [did he deal with] Saubha and Sālva? (BhP 10.78.13) and so forth, and due to the waiting for him?"
Pūrṇimā said with a smile, as it were: "I do not know;
these are the workings of his yogic illusion (yogamāyā).
Just as this was displayed immediately after the deluding of Brahmā."

"O King, even though one year had passed since the departure of their lord of life, the children, struck by the illusory power of Kṛṣṇa, considered it to be only half a moment. [10.14.43] Vṛndā said: "In that case, tell me what was done by Hari for a long time after He returned to Vraja."
Was that not known by the residents of Dvārakā?
